category: External Interfaces II: External Languages, Processes, wolframscript, J/Link, .NET/Link, WSTP & LibraryLink
description: The ExternalEvaluate systems (Python, NodeJS, Julia, R, Ruby, Java, Octave, Shell, SQL, Jupyter), session and object handling, external storage and code runners, operating-system process control (ProcessObject, pipes, kill, system open), remote evaluation on other machines and batch clusters, and the wolframscript command-line switches not covered in the basic scripting chunk; plus the compiled-language and VM bridges: J/Link, .NET/Link, WSTP link functions, LibraryLink, the foreign function interface with raw memory, CUDALink and the CCompilerDriver build loop.

tools.name: Python
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for CPython: ExternalEvaluate["Python", code] runs code in a fresh or persistent session (StartExternalSession["Python"]), converting Python numbers, strings, lists, dicts, NumPy arrays and pandas objects to Wolfram expressions and back; ExternalFunction wraps a Python function, and "Python" -> <|"Executable" -> path|> or a registered evaluator selects the interpreter and virtual environment. Python packages (numpy, pandas, pyzmq) are used for data conversion.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["Python", "1 + 1"]
session = StartExternalSession["Python"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "import numpy as np\nnp.linspace(0, 1, 5)"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "x = <* 3 + 4 *>"] (* template insertion of Wolfram values *)
ExternalEvaluate["Python" -> <|"Executable" -> "C:\\venv\\Scripts\\python.exe"|>, code]
f = ExternalFunction[session, "def sq(x): return x*x"]; f[5]
DeleteObject[session]

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: Python source string, File[...] or a {"Function" -> ..., "Arguments" -> ...} association for calling a function.

parameters.name: Executable
parameters.description: Path to a specific Python interpreter.

tools.notes: RegisterExternalEvaluator adds interpreters not found automatically; FindExternalEvaluators lists detected ones. Objects that cannot be converted come back as ExternalObject handles.

tools.name: NodeJS
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for JavaScript via Node.js: runs snippets or files in a Node session, converting JSON-compatible values to Wolfram expressions (arrays, associations, numbers, strings) and supporting ExternalFunction for JS functions and npm modules installed in the session's environment. Useful for JSON tooling, JavaScript libraries and testing code destined for the web.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["NodeJS", "[1,2,3].map(x => x*2)"]
session = StartExternalSession["NodeJS"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "const crypto = require('crypto'); crypto.randomUUID()"]
ExternalFunction[session, "(a, b) => a + b"][2, 3]

tools.name: Julia
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for Julia (needs the Julia executable and its Wolfram-related packages installed): evaluates code in a Julia session with automatic conversion of numbers, arrays, strings, tuples and dictionaries, and ExternalFunction for calling Julia functions. Good for delegating high-performance numerical loops to Julia while orchestrating from Wolfram Language.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["Julia", "sum(1:100)"]
session = StartExternalSession["Julia"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "using LinearAlgebra; det([1 2; 3 4])"]
ExternalFunction[session, "x -> x^2"][4]

tools.name: R
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for R: evaluates R code in a session (requires R plus the RLink-style bridge packages), converting vectors, matrices, data frames and lists to Wolfram lists/associations/Datasets, and exposing R functions through ExternalFunction. Use it for statistical procedures available only as R packages (CRAN) while keeping the workflow in Wolfram Language.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["R", "mean(c(1,2,3))"]
session = StartExternalSession["R"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "library(stats); t.test(rnorm(20), mu = 0)$p.value"]
ExternalFunction[session, "function(x) sd(x)"][{1, 2, 3, 4}]

tools.name: Shell
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for the operating-system shell (bash/zsh/sh on Unix, cmd on Windows): each evaluation returns an ExternalEvaluate result object or association with "StandardOutput", "StandardError" and "ExitCode", and a persistent session keeps environment variables and the working directory between commands. RunProcess (listed) is the lower-level alternative for single commands with explicit argument lists.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["Shell", "ls -la"]
session = StartExternalSession["Shell"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "cd /tmp && export X=1"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "echo $X"]
ExternalEvaluate["Shell" -> "Bash", "uname -a"]

tools.name: SQL
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for SQL databases: ExternalEvaluate["SQL" -> ref, query] runs a query against a DatabaseReference (SQLite file, PostgreSQL, MySQL...) returning a Dataset, and "SQL-JDBC" uses JDBC drivers; parameters can be inserted with templates or the {"Command" -> sql, "Parameters" -> ...} form. It is the quickest way to run ad-hoc SQL without the entity layer.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["SQL" -> DatabaseReference[File["db.sqlite"]], "SELECT * FROM t LIMIT 5"]
session = StartExternalSession["SQL" -> ref]
ExternalEvaluate[session, "SELECT name, price FROM products WHERE price > 10"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, <|"Command" -> "SELECT * FROM t WHERE id = ?", "Parameters" -> {42}|>]
ExternalEvaluate["SQL-JDBC" -> <|"Backend" -> "PostgreSQL", ...|>, query]
tools.example:
db = DatabaseReference[File["chinook.sqlite"]];
ExternalEvaluate["SQL" -> db, "SELECT Name, Milliseconds FROM Track ORDER BY Milliseconds DESC LIMIT 3"]

tools.name: Java
tools.description: ExternalEvaluate system for Java (and "Jupyter" for any Jupyter kernel, "Ruby" and "Octave" for those languages): evaluates snippets through a JShell-style session or a Jupyter kernel, with standard value conversion. For deep Java integration (object handles, GUIs, class loading) use J/Link instead; ExternalEvaluate["Java", ...] is for quick one-off calls.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluate["Java", "Math.sqrt(2)"]
ExternalEvaluate["Ruby", "[1,2,3].sum"]
ExternalEvaluate["Octave", "eig([1 2; 3 4])"]
ExternalEvaluate["Jupyter" -> <|"Kernel" -> "ir"|>, code]
tools.example:
ExternalEvaluate["Octave", "x = linspace(0, 1, 5); x.^2"]
ExternalEvaluate["Ruby", "require 'json'; JSON.parse('{\"k\": 1}')"]

tools.name: ExternalSessionObject
tools.description: The object returned by StartExternalSession representing a running external interpreter; query it for "System", "Executable", "Version", "ProcessID", "SessionTime", evaluate with ExternalEvaluate[session, code], list active sessions with ExternalSessions[] and terminate with DeleteObject. Sessions persist state (imports, variables) between evaluations and should be closed explicitly.
tools.usage:
session = StartExternalSession["Python"]
session["Version"]
session["ProcessID"]
ExternalSessions[]
DeleteObject[session]

tools.name: ExternalObject
tools.description: Handle to an object living in an external session that could not be converted to a Wolfram expression (a Python class instance, file handle, model...); it can be passed back into ExternalEvaluate/ExternalFunction calls, inspected with ExternalValue[session, "name"] for named variables, and its methods called through ExternalFunction. ExternalOperation builds symbolic operations on external objects.
tools.usage:
obj = ExternalEvaluate[session, "open('f.txt')"]
ExternalEvaluate[session, obj, "read"]
ExternalValue[session, "variable"]
ExternalFunction[session, "str"][obj]

parameters.name: name
parameters.description: Variable name in the external session.

tools.name: ExternalEvaluators
tools.description: Lists the external evaluator installations known to the system (as a Dataset of system, version, executable), the newer form of FindExternalEvaluators (listed); RegisterExternalEvaluator (listed) and UnregisterExternalEvaluator manage custom entries such as a virtual-environment Python. Use it to diagnose which interpreter ExternalEvaluate will pick.
tools.usage:
ExternalEvaluators[]
ExternalEvaluators["Python"]
RegisterExternalEvaluator["Python", "C:\\venv\\Scripts\\python.exe"]
UnregisterExternalEvaluator["Python", path]
tools.example: ExternalEvaluators["Python"][All, {"Version", "Executable", "Registered"}]

tools.name: ExternalStorageUpload
tools.description: Uploads files or expressions to an external storage service (IPFS by default, Dropbox and others through ServiceConnect) returning an ExternalStorageObject; ExternalStorageDownload retrieves content by object or identifier and ExternalIdentifier represents identifiers in external systems (IPFS hashes, DOIs, Wikidata IDs). Used for decentralized/shared storage and for linking Wolfram data to external identifiers.
tools.usage:
obj = ExternalStorageUpload[File["data.csv"]]
obj = ExternalStorageUpload[expr, "IPFS"]
ExternalStorageDownload[obj]
ExternalStorageDownload[ExternalIdentifier["IPFS", "Qm..."]]
ExternalIdentifier["DOI", "10.1000/xyz"]

parameters.name: content
parameters.description: File, expression or list of files.

tools.name: ProcessObject
tools.description: Represents an OS process started with StartProcess (listed): ProcessStatus gives "Running"/"Finished", ProcessInformation returns exit code, PID and timing, ProcessConnection[proc, "StandardInput"|"StandardOutput"|"StandardError"] gives streams for interactive I/O (WriteLine/ReadLine/ReadString), KillProcess terminates it and Processes[] lists running processes. This is the toolkit for driving interactive command-line programs.
tools.usage:
proc = StartProcess[{"program", "arg1"}]
ProcessStatus[proc]
ProcessInformation[proc]
ProcessInformation[proc, "ExitCode"]
WriteLine[proc, "input"]
ReadLine[proc]
ReadString[ProcessConnection[proc, "StandardError"], EndOfBuffer]
KillProcess[proc]
Processes[]

tools.name: RunThrough
tools.description: RunThrough["command", expr] pipes the InputForm of expr to an external command's stdin and reads the command's stdout back as a Wolfram expression - a quick filter-style integration; SystemOpen opens a file, directory or URL with the operating system's default application (browser, viewer). Both are convenience wrappers around OS facilities.
tools.usage:
RunThrough["command", expr]
SystemOpen["file.pdf"]
SystemOpen["https://www.wolfram.com"]
SystemOpen[$TemporaryDirectory]

parameters.name: command
parameters.description: Shell command reading stdin and writing stdout.

tools.example:
RunThrough["sort -n", Column[{3, 1, 2}]]
Export["report.pdf", nb]; SystemOpen["report.pdf"]

tools.name: RemoteRun
tools.description: Runs a shell command on a remote machine over SSH (RemoteRun returns the exit code, RemoteRunProcess an association with output, error and exit code), using a host string or a RemoteConnectionObject from RemoteConnect with stored credentials; RemoteFile references files on the remote host for Import/Export/CopyFile. Use them for orchestrating jobs on servers and clusters.
tools.usage:
RemoteRun["user@host", "command"]
RemoteRunProcess["user@host", "command"]
conn = RemoteConnect["host", "user", "password"]
RemoteRunProcess[conn, {"ls", "-la"}]
CopyFile["local.csv", RemoteFile["user@host:/data/local.csv"]]
Import[RemoteFile["user@host:/data/result.json"]]

parameters.name: Authentication
parameters.description: Option: password or SSH key (<|"SSHKey" -> File[...]|>).

tools.name: RemoteEvaluate
tools.description: Evaluates a Wolfram Language expression on a remote kernel reached over SSH (host string, RemoteKernelObject or list of hosts for parallel evaluation), returning the result locally; RemoteKernelObject represents a persistent remote kernel that keeps definitions between calls. It is the simplest way to use a bigger machine or a licensed remote kernel from a local session.
tools.usage:
RemoteEvaluate["user@host", expr]
RemoteEvaluate[{"host1", "host2"}, expr]
kernel = RemoteKernelObject["user@host"]
RemoteEvaluate[kernel, expr]
RemoteEvaluate[host, expr, Authentication -> <|"SSHKey" -> File[...]|>]

parameters.name: host
parameters.description: SSH host specification, RemoteKernelObject or list of hosts.

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Expression to evaluate remotely (held; use With to inject local values).

tools.notes: Requires a Wolfram kernel installed on the remote host; introduced in 12.2.

tools.name: RemoteBatchSubmit
tools.description: Submits an expression as a batch job to a cloud or HPC batch system (AWS Batch, Azure Batch, Slurm/PBS-style environments described by RemoteBatchSubmissionEnvironment), returning a RemoteBatchJobObject whose status, output and logs can be queried; RemoteBatchMapSubmit maps a function over a list as an array job and RemoteBatchJobs lists jobs. Use it for large parameter sweeps that exceed local resources.
tools.usage:
env = RemoteBatchSubmissionEnvironment["AWSBatch", <|"JobQueue" -> "...", "JobDefinition" -> "..."|>]
job = RemoteBatchSubmit[env, expr]
job = RemoteBatchSubmit[env, expr, RemoteProviderSettings -> <|"VCPUCount" -> 8|>]
job["JobStatus"]
job["EvaluationResult"]
RemoteBatchMapSubmit[env, f, {x1, x2, ...}]
RemoteBatchJobs[env]
RemoteBatchJobAbort[job]

parameters.name: expr
parameters.description: Expression evaluated in the batch job (held).

parameters.name: TimeConstraint / RemoteProviderSettings
parameters.description: Options controlling job limits and provider resources.

tools.notes: Introduced in 12.2; requires provider credentials (e.g. AWS keys via ServiceConnect).

tools.name: wolframscript -format
tools.description: Selects how wolframscript serializes the result of -code/-file/-function: "InputForm" (default), "Text"/"OutputForm", "JSON", "ExpressionJSON", "TeX", "Image"/"PNG", "WXF", "CSV"... Combine with -o file to write the result to a file; for JSON the result must be convertible (associations become objects).
tools.usage:
wolframscript -code "expr" -format JSON
wolframscript -code "Plot[Sin[x],{x,0,6}]" -format PNG -o plot.png
wolframscript -file script.wl -format Text

parameters.name: -o file / -output file
parameters.description: Write the result to a file instead of stdout.

tools.example:
wolframscript -code "<|\"primes\"->Prime[Range[5]]|>" -format JSON
(* {"primes":[2,3,5,7,11]} *)

tools.name: wolframscript -print
tools.description: Prints the result of every top-level expression in a -file run (not just the last), or with -print all also results of expressions inside CompoundExpressions; combined with -verbose it shows progress. Use it to convert exploratory files into batch runs that echo each result.
tools.usage:
wolframscript -file script.wl -print
wolframscript -file script.wl -print all
wolframscript -file script.wl -verbose

parameters.name: -verbose
parameters.description: Print diagnostic information about kernel start-up and evaluation.

tools.example: wolframscript -print -file analysis.wl > results.txt

tools.name: wolframscript -api
tools.description: Calls a deployed cloud APIFunction by UUID or URL from the command line, passing parameters with -args (key=value pairs) and printing the response; -cloud selects the cloud base and -authenticate stores credentials for non-interactive use. Lets shell scripts and CI jobs call Wolfram Cloud APIs without a local kernel licence.
tools.usage:
wolframscript -api <uuid-or-url> -args n=5
wolframscript -cloud -api https://www.wolframcloud.com/obj/user/nthprime -args n=1000
wolframscript -authenticate user@example.com password
wolframscript -disconnect

parameters.name: -api id
parameters.description: Cloud object UUID or URL of an APIFunction.

parameters.name: -authenticate
parameters.description: Store Wolfram ID credentials for cloud access.

tools.example: wolframscript -api 5e6f...-uuid -args city=Paris days=3

tools.name: wolframscript -timeout
tools.description: Limits the evaluation time (seconds) of a wolframscript run, aborting with a non-zero exit code when exceeded; -charset sets the character encoding of input/output (e.g. UTF-8), -linkmode/-linkname connect to an existing kernel, and -version / -h print version and help. Useful guards for unattended batch jobs.
tools.usage:
wolframscript -code "expr" -timeout 60
wolframscript -file script.wl -charset UTF8
wolframscript -version
wolframscript -h
tools.example: wolframscript -timeout 300 -file nightly.wl || echo "job failed or timed out"

tools.name: wolframscript -configure
tools.description: Sets persistent wolframscript configuration keys: WOLFRAMSCRIPT_KERNELPATH (which kernel executable to use), WOLFRAMSCRIPT_CLOUDBASE (default cloud) and others, stored in the user's configuration; without arguments it prints the current settings. Use it on machines with several Wolfram installations or a private cloud.
tools.usage:
wolframscript -configure
wolframscript -configure WOLFRAMSCRIPT_KERNELPATH="C:\Program Files\Wolfram Research\Wolfram\15.0\WolframKernel.exe"
wolframscript -configure WOLFRAMSCRIPT_CLOUDBASE=https://cloud.mycompany.com
tools.example: wolframscript -configure WOLFRAMSCRIPT_KERNELPATH=/usr/local/Wolfram/Mathematica/14.2/Executables/WolframKernel

tools.name: wolframscript -activate
tools.description: Activates the local Wolfram Engine/kernel licence from the command line (interactive or with -entitlement/-activationkey arguments), required before wolframscript can start a local kernel on a fresh installation (e.g. the free Wolfram Engine in Docker images). Errors such as 'Your Wolfram product is not activated' point here.
tools.usage:
wolframscript -activate
wolframscript -activate -entitlement O-WSTD-...
wolframscript -username user@example.com -password pw -activate
wolframscript -deactivate
tools.example: wolframscript -activate  # then follow the prompts

tools.name: wolfram -wstp
tools.description: Starts the kernel executable (wolfram / WolframKernel / math) as a WSTP server so that an external program or another kernel can connect to it: LinkLaunch["wolfram -wstp"] from Wolfram Language, or the C/Java/.NET/Python client libraries. Other useful kernel switches: -noprompt, -run "expr", -initfile file, -script file, -pwfile, -mathlink (legacy alias) and -noinit.
tools.usage:
wolfram -wstp
wolfram -wstp -linkmode listen -linkname 9000 -linkprotocol TCPIP
wolfram -noprompt -run "Print[1+1]; Exit[]"
wolfram -noinit -script file.wl
LinkLaunch["wolfram -wstp"]

parameters.name: -wstp
parameters.description: Run as a WSTP link endpoint.

parameters.name: -linkmode / -linkname / -linkprotocol
parameters.description: Link connection settings (Launch, Listen, Connect; TCPIP, SharedMemory).

parameters.name: -noinit
parameters.description: Skip init.m files for a clean start.

tools.name: Wolfram Client Library for Python
tools.description: The official Python package wolframclient (pip install wolframclient): WolframLanguageSession starts a local kernel, WolframCloudSession calls the cloud, session.evaluate runs expressions built with wl (symbolic constructors) or wlexpr (source strings), results convert to native Python types, session.function wraps a Wolfram function as a Python callable, and WXF serialization (export/binary_deserialize) moves large arrays efficiently. It is the recommended way to drive Mathematica from Python programs and services.
tools.usage:
from wolframclient.evaluation import WolframLanguageSession
from wolframclient.language import wl, wlexpr
session = WolframLanguageSession()
session.evaluate(wlexpr('Integrate[Sin[x]^2, x]'))
session.evaluate(wl.Total([1, 2, 3]))
f = session.function(wl.Prime); f(10)
session.terminate()

parameters.name: kernel
parameters.description: Optional path to the WolframKernel executable when not auto-detected.

tools.example:
from wolframclient.evaluation import WolframLanguageSession
from wolframclient.language import wl
with WolframLanguageSession() as s:
    print(s.evaluate(wl.NIntegrate(wl.Exp(-wl.Power(wl.Global.x, 2)), [wl.Global.x, -10, 10])))

tools.name: InstallService
tools.description: Installs a Wolfram Language service description (a paclet or file defining custom ServiceConnect requests for a REST API) so that ServiceConnect["MyService"] becomes available; it is the mechanism for wrapping in-house web APIs with authentication into ServiceObject connections that behave like the built-in ones.
tools.usage:
InstallService["path/to/service.m"]
InstallService[File["MyService.paclet"]]
ServiceConnect["MyService"]

tools.name: InstallJava
tools.description: J/Link (Needs["JLink`"]): InstallJava launches (or connects to) the Java runtime bundled with Mathematica and prepares the bridge; ReinstallJava restarts it (e.g. with a different class path or heap size via JVMArguments) and UninstallJava shuts it down. Must be called before JavaNew/LoadJavaClass, though most J/Link functions call it automatically.
tools.usage:
Needs["JLink`"]
InstallJava[]
ReinstallJava[JVMArguments -> "-Xmx4g"]
ReinstallJava[ClassPath -> "C:\\libs\\mylib.jar"]
UninstallJava[]

parameters.name: JVMArguments
parameters.description: Option: extra JVM flags (heap size, system properties).

tools.notes: Package functions in the JLink` context, not System symbols.

tools.name: JavaNew
tools.description: J/Link: JavaNew["class", args] constructs a Java object and returns a JavaObject handle whose methods and fields are called with obj@method[args] and obj@field; LoadJavaClass loads a class so its static methods become callable as Class`method[...]; MakeJavaObject converts Wolfram values (strings, numbers, arrays) into Java objects; JavaObjectQ tests handles and ReleaseJavaObject frees them (or wrap code in JavaBlock for automatic release). AddToClassPath adds jars or directories at runtime.
tools.usage:
obj = JavaNew["java.util.ArrayList"]
obj@add["item"]
obj@size[]
LoadJavaClass["java.lang.Math"]
Math`sqrt[2.]
MakeJavaObject[{1, 2, 3}]
AddToClassPath["C:\\libs"]
JavaBlock[ ... ]
ReleaseJavaObject[obj]
tools.notes: Java exceptions surface as Java::excptn messages; use JavaShow to display Java GUI windows created from Wolfram Language.

tools.name: JavaShow
tools.description: J/Link: JavaShow brings a Java window (Frame, JFrame, Dialog) to the front so Swing/AWT GUIs built from Wolfram Language are visible; together with DoModal/EndModal for modal event loops and JavaObjectToExpression / ReturnAsJavaObject for controlling result conversion it supports building Java user interfaces and using Java libraries with callbacks into the kernel.
tools.usage:
JavaShow[frame]
DoModal[]
EndModal[]
ReturnAsJavaObject[expr]
JavaObjectToExpression[obj]

tools.name: InstallNET
tools.description: .NET/Link (Windows; Needs["NETLink`"]): InstallNET starts the .NET runtime bridge, LoadNETAssembly loads an assembly (DLL or GAC name) and LoadNETType a type so its static members are callable, NETNew constructs objects (methods via obj@Method[args], properties via obj@Property), MakeNETObject converts Wolfram values, NETTypeInfo lists members, ReleaseNETObject frees objects and NETBlock releases automatically; UninstallNET shuts down. Also exposes COM objects (CreateCOMObject) and Win32 DLL functions (DefineDLLFunction).
tools.usage:
Needs["NETLink`"]
InstallNET[]
LoadNETAssembly["System.Windows.Forms"]
LoadNETType["System.Math"]
Math`Sqrt[2.]
obj = NETNew["System.Text.StringBuilder"]
obj@Append["text"]
obj@ToString[]
NETTypeInfo["System.String"]
com = CreateCOMObject["Excel.Application"]
f = DefineDLLFunction["GetTickCount", "kernel32.dll", "int", {}]
tools.notes: Windows-only; useful for COM automation of Office applications and calling Win32 DLLs without LibraryLink.

tools.name: LinkLaunch
tools.description: Launches an external program (typically another Wolfram kernel or a WSTP-enabled executable) and opens a WSTP link to it, returning a LinkObject; LinkConnect connects to a link already listening (LinkCreate creates a listening link), LinkClose closes and Links[] lists open links. Links carry packets such as EvaluatePacket/ReturnPacket between programs - the protocol under parallel kernels, J/Link and the front end.
tools.usage:
link = LinkLaunch["wolfram -wstp"]
link = LinkCreate["name", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]
link = LinkConnect["port@host", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]
LinkClose[link]
Links[]
LinkInterrupt[link]

tools.name: LinkWrite
tools.description: Writes an expression (usually a packet: EvaluatePacket[expr], or a raw expression for custom programs) to a WSTP link, and LinkRead reads the next expression/packet sent back (ReturnPacket, TextPacket, MessagePacket, ...); LinkReadyQ tests whether data is waiting (with optional timeout), LinkReadHeld/LinkWriteHeld keep expressions unevaluated, and LinkPatterns lists the patterns an installed program handles. These are the primitives for hand-rolled kernel-to-program protocols.
tools.usage:
LinkWrite[link, Unevaluated[EvaluatePacket[expr]]]
LinkWrite[link, expr]
LinkRead[link]
LinkRead[link, Hold]
LinkReadyQ[link]
LinkReadyQ[link, timeout]
LinkPatterns[link]
tools.example:
LinkWrite[k, Unevaluated[EvaluatePacket[N[Pi, 30]]]];
If[LinkReadyQ[k, 10], LinkRead[k], "timeout"]

tools.name: Install
tools.description: Install["program"] launches a WSTP-enabled external program (built with wsprep/mprep templates in C, or J/Link/.NET/Link) and installs the functions it exports so they are callable as ordinary Wolfram functions; Uninstall terminates it. This is the classic MathLink/WSTP way to add C functions - LibraryLink (in-process) is faster for pure numerical code, Install keeps the program in a separate process (crash isolation, GUIs).
tools.usage:
link = Install["program"]
link = Install["path/to/addtwo"]
LinkPatterns[link]
Uninstall[link]

parameters.name: program
parameters.description: Executable built with the WSTP template system.

tools.name: LibraryFunction
tools.description: The object returned by LibraryFunctionLoad (listed) representing a function in a loaded shared library, callable like a Wolfram function with automatic argument checking (Integer, Real, Complex, {Real, 2} tensors, "UTF8String", True|False, LibraryDataType[Image], NumericArray, SparseArray); LibraryFunctionInformation shows its signature, LibraryFunctionUnload unloads it, LibraryLoad/LibraryUnload manage the library itself and FindLibrary locates a library by name on $LibraryPath. LibraryFunctionError is the failure form for library errors.
tools.usage:
f = LibraryFunctionLoad["lib", "func", {Real, {Real, 1}}, {Real, 1}]
f[2.0, {1., 2., 3.}]
LibraryFunctionInformation[f]
LibraryFunctionUnload[f]
LibraryLoad["lib"]
LibraryUnload["lib"]
FindLibrary["lib"]
$LibraryPath

parameters.name: func
parameters.description: Exported function name following the LibraryLink calling convention.

parameters.name: argtypes / rettype
parameters.description: Type specifications: Integer, Real, Complex, {type, rank} or {type, rank, "Shared"|"Constant"|"Manual"}, "UTF8String", "Boolean", LibraryDataType[...].

tools.example:
lib = FindLibrary["demo"]; (* from the LibraryLink examples *)
f = LibraryFunctionLoad[lib, "demo_I_I", {Integer}, Integer];
f[41] (* 42 *)
LibraryFunctionInformation[f]
tools.notes: Libraries are compiled against WolframLibrary.h in $InstallationDirectory/SystemFiles/IncludeFiles/C; CCompilerDriver` (CreateLibrary) compiles C source from Wolfram Language.

tools.name: LibraryFunctionDeclaration
tools.description: Declares a library function with typed signature for use inside FunctionCompile'd code (compiled code calls the C function directly, without kernel round trips); together with LibraryFunctionLoad's compiled-library workflow and FunctionCompileExportLibrary (listed) it lets the compiler both consume and produce shared libraries. Introduced in 12.2 for the new compiler.
tools.usage:
decl = LibraryFunctionDeclaration["cfun", "lib", {"CInt", "CDouble"} -> "CDouble"]
FunctionCompile[Function[Typed[x, "Real64"], cfun[2, x]], FunctionDeclarations -> {decl}]
FunctionDeclaration[name, Typed[...]]

parameters.name: cfun
parameters.description: Name used in compiled code (may differ from the exported symbol given as a rule).

parameters.name: types
parameters.description: C types such as "CInt", "CDouble", "CString", "CArray"[...] -> return type.

tools.name: ForeignFunctionLoad
tools.description: Foreign function interface (13.1+): loads a C function from any shared library by name and C-type signature without writing LibraryLink wrappers, returning a ForeignFunction callable with automatic conversion of integers, reals, strings and RawPointers; supports callbacks and struct types via the compiler's type system. Ideal for calling system libraries (libc, Win32, OpenSSL) and existing C APIs directly.
tools.usage:
ff = ForeignFunctionLoad["lib", "func", {"CInt", "CDouble"} -> "CDouble"]
ff[2, 3.5]
ForeignFunctionLoad["libc", "getpid", {} -> "CInt"][]
ForeignFunctionLoad["kernel32", "GetTickCount64", {} -> "CUnsignedLongLong"][]

parameters.name: sig
parameters.description: {argtypes} -> rettype using C type names ("CInt", "CDouble", "CString", "RawPointer"::["CDouble"], "OpaqueRawPointer", struct types).

tools.notes: On Windows use library names such as "msvcrt" or "kernel32"; on macOS/Linux "libc"/"libm". Requires the compiler tools shipped with the product.

tools.name: RawMemoryAllocate
tools.description: Raw memory management for the foreign function interface: RawMemoryAllocate allocates a typed buffer returning a RawPointer, RawMemoryFree releases it, RawMemoryImport reads C data (arrays, strings, structs) into Wolfram expressions and RawMemoryExport writes Wolfram data into C memory; OpaqueRawPointer is an untyped pointer handle and ManagedObject/CreateManagedObject tie a pointer's lifetime to garbage collection. Needed when C functions take or return pointers.
tools.usage:
ptr = RawMemoryAllocate["CDouble", n]
RawMemoryExport[{1., 2., 3.}, "CDouble"]
RawMemoryImport[ptr, {"CDouble", n}]
RawMemoryImport[strPtr, "CString"]
RawMemoryFree[ptr]
RawPointer[address, "CDouble"]
OpaqueRawPointer[address]

tools.name: CUDAFunctionLoad
tools.description: CUDALink (Needs["CUDALink`"]): CUDAFunctionLoad compiles/loads a CUDA kernel from source or PTX and returns a CUDAFunction callable on Wolfram arrays or CUDAMemory objects; CUDAQ tests for a usable GPU, CUDAInformation describes devices, and CUDAMemoryLoad/CUDAMemoryGet move data. The package also provides ready-made GPU operations (CUDAFourier, CUDADot, CUDAImageConvolve, CUDAFold, CUDATranspose). OpenCLLink offers the same workflow for OpenCL devices (OpenCLFunctionLoad, OpenCLQ).
tools.usage:
Needs["CUDALink`"]
CUDAQ[]
CUDAInformation[]
kernel = CUDAFunctionLoad[src, "addTwo", {{_Real, _, "Input"}, {_Real, _, "Output"}, _Integer}, 256]
kernel[in, out, n]
mem = CUDAMemoryLoad[data]; CUDAMemoryGet[mem]
CUDAFourier[list]
Needs["OpenCLLink`"]; OpenCLQ[]

parameters.name: src
parameters.description: CUDA C source string, File or PTX.

tools.notes: Requires an NVIDIA GPU with CUDA toolkit; package functions in CUDALink`.

tools.name: EvaluatePacket
tools.description: The WSTP packet vocabulary for talking to a kernel over a raw link: EvaluatePacket[expr] requests evaluation, ReturnPacket[expr] carries the result, ReturnExpressionPacket the typeset-form result, TextPacket printed text, MessagePacket a message, InputNamePacket/OutputNamePacket the In/Out labels, and EnterTextPacket/EnterExpressionPacket emulate front-end input. Loop with LinkRead until a ReturnPacket arrives; the C/Java/Python client libraries hide this protocol.
tools.usage:
LinkWrite[link, Unevaluated[EvaluatePacket[expr]]]
LinkWrite[link, Unevaluated[EnterTextPacket["1+1"]]]
While[Head[p = LinkRead[link]] =!= ReturnPacket, handle[p]]
tools.example:
LinkWrite[k, Unevaluated[EvaluatePacket[Print["hi"]; 7]]];
results = Reap[While[Head[p = LinkRead[k]] =!= ReturnPacket, Sow[p]]] (* TextPacket["hi"] then ReturnPacket[7] *)

tools.name: LinkObject
tools.description: LinkObject[name, id, ...] represents an open WSTP link (as returned by LinkLaunch/LinkConnect/Install and listed by Links[]); $ParentLink is the link to the controlling program, LinkError reports the last link error, and LinkActivate completes a connection for links created with LinkCreate. Properties such as the protocol and name are visible in the object; use LinkClose to release.
tools.usage:
LinkObject["name", n, m]
Links[]
LinkError[link]
LinkActivate[link]
$ParentLink
tools.example:
Links[] (* {LinkObject[...], ...} *)
link = LinkCreate["9999", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]; (* wait for a client *) LinkActivate[link]

tools.name: CreateLibrary
tools.description: CCompilerDriver package (Needs["CCompilerDriver`"]): CreateLibrary compiles C/C++ source (string or files) into a shared library usable with LibraryFunctionLoad, using a detected compiler (CCompilers[] lists them; DefaultCCompiler); CreateExecutable builds stand-alone programs and CreateObjectFile object files. Options set include paths, libraries, defines and compiler flags. Together with LibraryFunctionLoad this gives an in-notebook C development loop.
tools.usage:
Needs["CCompilerDriver`"]
lib = CreateLibrary[src, "libname"]
lib = CreateLibrary[{"file1.c", "file2.c"}, "libname", "IncludeDirectories" -> {...}, "Libraries" -> {...}]
CCompilers[]
DefaultCCompiler[]
CreateExecutable[src, "prog"]

parameters.name: src
parameters.description: C source string or list of source files.

tools.name: WSTP C API
tools.description: The C-level Wolfram Symbolic Transfer Protocol library (wstp.h, formerly mathlink.h): WSInitialize/WSOpenArgcArgv open a link, WSPutFunction/WSPutInteger64/WSPutReal64/WSPutString/WSPutReal64Array send data, WSGetInteger64/WSGetReal64/WSGetString/WSGetReal64Array receive, WSNextPacket/WSNewPacket handle packets, WSEndPacket/WSFlush finish messages and WSClose/WSDeinitialize clean up; wsprep (formerly mprep) generates the glue code for Install-able programs from .tm template files. Libraries and headers live in $InstallationDirectory/SystemFiles/Links/WSTP/DeveloperKit.
tools.example:
cc prog.c -I"$WSTP/CompilerAdditions" -L"$WSTP/CompilerAdditions" -lWSTP64i4 -o prog
./prog   # prints Prime[100] = 541 computed by a launched kernel

tools.name: LinkProtocol
tools.description: Option of LinkLaunch, LinkCreate, LinkConnect and LaunchKernels choosing the transport: "SharedMemory" (default local, fastest), "TCPIP" (network, with name "port@host"), "Pipes" (Unix); together with LinkMode (Launch/Listen/Connect, set by the kernel command-line switches) and the link name they define how two programs find each other. Use TCPIP links to run kernels on other machines or through firewalls.
tools.usage:
LinkCreate["8000", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]
LinkConnect["8000@192.168.1.10", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]
LinkLaunch["wolfram -wstp", LinkProtocol -> "SharedMemory"]
tools.example:
(* machine A *) link = LinkCreate["8000", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]
(* machine B *) k = LinkConnect["8000@machineA", LinkProtocol -> "TCPIP"]
